chunks: Passive components' parasitics. The question: Passive components' parasitics.
A real resistor, capacitor (a part that stores charge) or inductor (a coil that resists changes in current) is never purely that one thing.
Each also contains small amounts of the other two, caused by its shape, wire legs (leads) and materials. These unwanted extras are called parasitics.
They are small at low frequency, but at high frequency they take over and make the part behave differently from its label.
Think of a spring from a hardware store. In theory it only stretches and pushes back. In reality, the metal also has weight, and it rubs a little as it moves.
Move it slowly and you only notice the springiness. Shake it very fast and the weight dominates.
A capacitor is the same: at high enough frequency, its hidden inductance matters more than its capacitance.
At low frequency the capacitor is an open circuit and the inductor a short, so you see R.
At high frequency C p shunts the resistor and the part becomes capacitive; for a large R the C p effect arrives first.
Parasitic: an unwanted extra property, like stray inductance in a capacitor. ESR: equivalent series resistance, the small resistance hidden inside a capacitor.
ESL: equivalent series inductance, the small inductance of a capacitor's leads and plates. DCR: the resistance of an inductor's copper wire to steady (DC) current.
Self-resonant frequency: where a part's hidden inductance and capacitance cancel and it stops acting like itself.
A 100 nanofarads capacitor has about 0. 5 nanohenries of ESL. Its capacitance and ESL cancel each other (resonate) at 1 over (2 pi square root of LC ) , about 22 megahertz.
Below that, it acts as a capacitor and works as you drew it. Above 22 megahertz it acts as an inductor, so it no longer soaks up fast noise the way the schematic suggests.
That is the whole idea.
"Every real passive has the other two elements in it. A resistor has a little series inductance and a little shunt capacitance.
A capacitor has ESR and ESL, so above its self-resonant frequency, around 20 megahertz for a small 100 nanofarads part, it acts like an inductor.
An inductor has winding resistance and winding capacitance, so above its self-resonance it acts like a capacitor.
They come from geometry: lead length, plate loops, and turn-to-turn spacing. So I always check the impedance curve, not just the nominal value."
